title: Termination of linear-constraint loops
formal: Determine separately, for each state domain \(D\in\{\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R\}\), whether termination of single-path linear-constraint loops over \(D\) is decidable. An input is \(d\ge1\) and an explicitly given system of rational linear inequalities \[A x+B y\le c,\qquad A,B\in\mathbb Q^{m\times d},\quad c\in\mathbb Q^m,\] defining allowed consecutive states \(x,y\in D^d\). Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine for that fixed domain which always halts and decides whether \[\neg\exists (x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in(D^d)^{\mathbb N}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\qquad A x_n+B x_{n+1}\le c?\] Thus termination means that every execution from every initial state is finite, irrespective of the allowed successor choices. The three domain variants are retained separately, with no assumption that their decidability statuses coincide.
why: This question asks how much nondeterminism can be introduced into elementary linear dynamics while preserving decidable universal termination. A single system of inequalities allows infinitely many possible successors but retains a strong convex structure over the reals. Resolving its domain-specific cases would locate a central boundary between complete verification algorithms for affine programs and undecidability in more expressive program models.
status_note: Explicitly open over integers, rationals and reals in Carelli’s ICALP 2026 introduction and in Open Problem 2 of the survey revised 24 July 2026. The 2024 two-variable theorem is over real states; the 2026 one-variable integer theorem is conditional on a generalized Collatz conjecture. Neither resolves the unrestricted domain family. Bounded checking on 16 September 2026 found no matching later resolution, without independently verifying every cited proof.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

importance.reason: A central longstanding termination question at a sharply defined model boundary. The source family distinguishes integer, rational and real executions, and 2026 results connect even the one-variable integer case to unresolved generalized Collatz behavior.

sentences: A single-path linear-constraint loop permits exactly those successive state pairs satisfying one finite conjunction of rational linear inequalities.
Termination means that no infinite execution exists from any initial state under any allowed sequence of choices.
The question asks for the decidability status separately over integer, rational and real state spaces, with unrestricted dimension.
Affine subclasses and the two-variable real case are decidable, while a 2026 result for one integer variable remains conditional on a generalized Collatz conjecture.
A resolution would locate the algorithmic boundary between deterministic affine dynamics and more general nondeterministic linear programs.

definitions: Here \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), \(m\ge0\), and all inequalities are non-strict and componentwise. The system describes one conjunction, equivalently one closed rational polyhedron in \(\mathbb R^{2d}\); no disjunction of different transition relations is permitted. Over integers or rationals, allowed transitions are the points of this same polyhedron in \(D^{2d}\). The state variables are unbounded, and all coordinates are chosen simultaneously. From \(x\), any \(y\) satisfying the conjunction may be the next state. If there is no such \(y\), the finite execution stops. There is no probabilistic or fairness condition; the existence of even one infinite sequence is nontermination. A guard involving only \(x\) is included as rows with zero \(y\)-coefficients. Equality is represented by two inequalities. If \(m=0\), every pair is allowed and the loop is nonterminating. All initial states in \(D^d\) are considered; no supplied initial-state region or fixed starting value is part of the input. Both \(d\) and the number of inequalities are unrestricted. Every rational coefficient is encoded as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator in explicit finite matrix lists. Multiplying each row by a positive common denominator gives an equivalent integer-coefficient input, over each domain separately. The machine receives only finite rational data, even for the real-state case; states themselves are not encoded as extra machine inputs. For each domain the required machine must be uniform in dimension and coefficients, with no oracle, random error or complexity bound. Termination does not require a common bound on the lengths of all finite executions.
answer_criterion: Give complete Lean-checked decidability or undecidability results for all three stated domain variants, recording each outcome separately. For a positive result, provide a total computable classifier on the finite rational descriptions and prove equivalence with absence of an infinite execution over the selected domain. For a negative result, prove that no such decider exists for that domain. Positive results for affine assignments, restricted dimensions or restricted inequalities alone are partial. An undecidability result for a subclass with the same rational input and selected state domain suffices for that domain; a proof allowing irrational coefficients or disjunctions changes the problem. A ranking-function search that can fail to return an answer is insufficient.

source_formulation.text: Determine decidability of termination for loops whose body is a conjunction of linear constraints between the current and next state, beyond the affine-assignment case.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question; domain variants made explicit

context_blocks.text: An affine assignment specifies one successor. A relational loop may admit a whole set of successors, and termination has to survive every permitted choice from every starting point. The finite description is still only a conjunction of linear inequalities; it does not contain a program with arbitrary branching or a supplied unbounded computation.

The original survey discusses termination across integer, rational and real state spaces before presenting the general relational question. The July 2026 survey makes the distinction explicit in Open Problem 2. The card therefore keeps the three cases as separate targets within the same family, rather than selecting one domain silently or assuming a transfer between them.

Universal termination permits arbitrarily long finite executions as the initial state varies. For example, the integer relation requiring a positive current value and decreasing it by one terminates from every start, although there is no bound valid for all positive starts. The displayed predicate instead rules out every infinite execution.

The affine subclass is decidable over all three domains. Allowing a finite disjunction of transition polyhedra leads to a different multipath model with undecidability results. The open single-path class lies between these settings: its choices arise from one conjunction, not an unrestricted union of branches.

Guilmant and coauthors decide the problem for at most two real-valued variables. This theorem fixes both a dimension bound and the real domain; it is not a theorem about two integer variables or arbitrary dimension. Distinguishing those hypotheses is essential when comparing nearby positive results.

Carelli’s ICALP 2026 paper retains the general question and investigates a single integer variable. Its polynomial-time termination result is conditional on a precisely stated generalized Collatz reachability conjecture. Deciding cycles is not enough by itself, because an infinite trace can keep visiting new states. Thus the paper does not supply an unconditional algorithm for the domain family here.
